text: Your body clock keeps running without daylight, but it drifts. Michel Siffre spent two months alone in a cave with no clock and no sunlight, and his sleep-and-wake rhythm settled into a day slightly longer than 24 hours.
more: He also lost count. When his team told him the two months were up, Siffre thought about a month less had gone by. Left to itself a body keeps decent time, but a mind keeps a terrible calendar.

text: There is no single settled answer for why you sleep. The strongest evidence points at memory. The patterns your brain fired while learning get replayed overnight, and people tested after a night's sleep beat people tested after the same gap awake.

Overnight, your brain gets rinsed out. The cells shrink back, the gaps between them widen, and fluid washes through carrying off the day's waste. The flow is far stronger asleep than it ever is awake.
more: It was first traced in mice, with dye pumped through and filmed. Among the trash being carried off are the proteins that clog up the brains of people with dementia, which is one reason a missed night is not free.

text: Roughly every 90 minutes your eyes start darting about under closed lids. Your brain is running almost as hard as it does awake. That is when most dreaming happens, about two hours a night. Your muscles are switched off, so you cannot act it out.
more: Wake somebody during one of those bursts and about four times in five they report a dream. Wake them between bursts and they usually have nothing. Everyone dreams. Most of it is simply never filed.

text: Light sets your body clock, but not through the cells you see with. A separate set of cells sits at the back of your eye. All they do is report how bright it is. They report straight to a small clump of cells in the middle of your brain. That clump keeps the schedule.

A newborn sleeps 14 to 17 hours out of 24, in scraps of two or three hours at a time. A teenager needs 8 to 10 hours in one block. The amount you need drops steadily while you grow, then stops changing for the rest of your life.

Melatonin is the hormone that tells your body it is night. Measured in a lab, its evening rise arrives one to two hours later in a teenager than in a younger child. A teenager still wide awake at eleven is following a clock, not dodging one.
Falling asleep for as little as fifteen seconds can hand you an answer you could not find awake.
tryit: Sit in a chair holding a spoon over a metal tray, and let yourself doze. The moment you genuinely drop off, your grip goes and the clatter wakes you. Edison and the painter Salvador Dali both napped this way on purpose.
more: Researchers tested it properly. They gave volunteers a math puzzle with a hidden shortcut in it. Volunteers who had dipped into that first shallow stage of sleep spotted the shortcut 83% of the time. Volunteers who stayed awake managed 30%. Sinking into deeper sleep wiped the advantage out.

text: Rest is written into the very first week of Genesis: six days of work, and a seventh set aside. Your body keeps a smaller version of the same pattern every single night, and it will not let you skip it for long.

Nobody has ever counted the cells in a body. The best estimate measures the size and packing of about 1,200 kinds of cell across 60 tissues, then adds it all up. That gives roughly 36 trillion in an adult man. It gives 28 trillion in an adult woman, and about 17 trillion in a ten-year-old.
more: Nine out of ten of those are red blood cells, which are tiny. Count by weight instead of by number and muscle and fat take over completely. Which answer is the right one depends entirely on what you are asking.

text: Coiled inside almost every one of your cells is about 6 ft (2 m) of DNA, spelled out in an alphabet of four letters and three billion letters long. All of it is folded into a nucleus far too small to see.

Every cell carries the whole instruction book and reads only its own chapter. A skin cell holds the full directions for building a heart and never opens them. A code that stores itself, copies itself and checks its own spelling reads like something written, not something spilled.
Your longest cell runs from the base of your spine all the way down to your big toe. That is over 3 ft (1 m) of one single cell.
more: At the other end of the scale, you could line about ten red blood cells side by side across the width of one hair from your head. Both are cells, and one is a million times bigger than the other.

text: You throw away and rebuild around 330 billion cells a day. The lining of your gut is the quickest of the lot, swapping its whole surface out every four or five days. Red blood cells last about four months.
You are about 60% water. Your brain and your heart are 73% water, your lungs 83%, your skin 64%, and even your bones come in at 31%.
more: Babies are the wettest of all, roughly 78% water at birth and drying out to about 65% by their first birthday. That is part of why a small child gets dangerously thirsty far faster than a grown-up does.

text: A few of your cells are the originals. The ones in the middle of the lens of each eye formed before you were born. They are never swapped out. They have to stay perfectly see-through for a whole lifetime.

Inside each cell sit hundreds of tiny power plants called mitochondria. They turn food and oxygen into energy the cell can use. A heart muscle cell crams in thousands of them, filling about a third of the cell. It never gets a night off.
Hold your breath and you soon feel a desperate need to gasp. That is mostly your body reacting to waste gas piling up. It is not you running out of oxygen.
tryit: Breathe in, hold it, and count. Then breathe all the way out and hold that, and count again. The empty one is far shorter. With no air in your lungs to dilute it, the carbon dioxide your cells keep making builds up much faster.

text: Your voice is two small flaps in your throat slapping together. A child's voice runs at about 285 slaps a second, an adult woman's around 250, an adult man's around 145. Lower voice, slower flaps.
more: The flaps grow as you do. The vibrating edge measures about half an inch (12 to 17 mm) in an adult woman and three quarters of an inch (17 to 23 mm) in an adult man. Longer and heavier means slower, and slower means deeper.

text: During puberty a boy's vocal folds grow up to 60% longer and thicker. A girl's grow too, by up to about a third. Bigger, heavier flaps swing more slowly, and the voice drops.
more: The cracking in between is best read as a control problem. The equipment changes size faster than the brain updates its aim, so a note escapes an octave off before the settings catch up.

text: Newborns cry with an accent. Recordings made in their first days show French babies' cries mostly rising in pitch. German babies' cries mostly fall. Each one matches the tune of the language it had been hearing from inside.
more: Thirty French and thirty German newborns, 1,254 cries, every one measured for pitch shape. None of them could babble yet, let alone copy a word. The tune arrived first.

text: The best way to stop hiccups is to make your diaphragm pull hard while you swallow at the same moment. A stiff straw built to force exactly that stopped hiccups in nearly 92% of the people who tried it.
more: An American farmer named Charles Osborne started hiccupping while trying to lift a hog. He did not stop for 68 years. That is an estimated 430 million hiccups, and it is the longest bout on record. Nothing anyone tried worked. It finally quit on its own.

text: Nobody has settled why yawning is catching. Cooling the brain, sharpening attention and keeping a group in step have all been argued for, and none of them has enough evidence to close the case. What is not in doubt is that seeing a yawn makes you likelier to do one.
tryit: Yawn deliberately in front of somebody who is reading, and count how long until they yawn back. It works better on people who know you well, which is itself part of the puzzle.

text: Laughing is mostly not about jokes. Researchers recorded real conversations and counted. People were around 30 times likelier to laugh with company than alone. Only about one line in eight that got a laugh was even remotely funny.
more: The speaker usually laughs more than the audience does, dropping laughs into their own sentences like punctuation. People signing rather than speaking put them in the same places.

text: The loudest shout Guinness has measured is 122.4 decibels, set by an Australian town crier, Joseph McGrail-Bateup, on the single word 'now'. It left him hoarse for days. The loudest scream on record, 129 decibels, belongs to Jill Drake.
more: The mark he beat had stood since 1994, when a Northern Irish schoolteacher, Annalisa Flanagan, reached 121.7 decibels shouting the word 'quiet'. McGrail-Bateup needed seven goes to get past her.

text: A whisper does not use your voice at all. The flaps hold still, and you shape the hiss of moving air instead.
tryit: Rest two fingers lightly on the front of your throat and say your name out loud. You will feel a clear buzz. Now whisper it. The buzzing stops dead, but the words still come through fine.

text: In Genesis the first job handed to a man is naming the animals, one at a time. Speech turns up very early in that account. A newborn arrives with the whole apparatus already assembled. That is long before there is anything to say with it.
There are no muscles inside your fingers. Every bend and straighten is worked from a distance, by muscles in your palm and forearm hauling on cords called tendons that run down inside each finger.
tryit: Wrap your left hand around your right forearm just below the elbow, then wiggle your right fingers. You can feel the muscles doing the job several inches away from the fingers that are actually moving.

text: Your fingerprints were finished before you were born. The ridges buckle into place between about the tenth and sixteenth week in the womb. After that they never change. Identical twins share the same DNA, and they still have different prints.
tryit: Scribble a thick patch of pencil on paper, rub a fingertip in it, press clear tape onto the finger and stick the tape down on white paper. You have just lifted your own print.
more: A handful of families are born with no fingerprints at all, from a single change in one gene. It causes them no health trouble whatsoever. It just makes crossing borders extremely slow.

text: A finger whose nerve has been cut will not wrinkle in water. Doctors use that as a test: warm water for half an hour, and any fingertip that stays smooth has a nerve problem.
tryit: Fill a bowl with comfortably warm water, around 104°F (40°C), and rest the fingertips of one hand in it. Ridges usually show up somewhere between 10 and 40 minutes. Keep the other hand out and compare.
more: Photograph a wrinkled finger, dry it off, and soak it again a day later. The loops and ridges land in the same places. The blood vessels underneath barely shift position, so the creases they pull have nowhere else to go.

text: Your little finger does far more than it looks capable of. Measured on a grip meter, leaving it out of your grip costs about a third of your strength. Leaving out the ring finger costs about a fifth.
One of your fingers cannot move on its own, and it is not the one you would guess.
tryit: Put your palm flat on a table and fold your middle finger under, knuckle down on the wood. Now lift each finger in turn. Thumb, index and little finger all come up easily. The ring finger will not budge, because its tendon is tied to the middle finger's.

text: Fingernails grow about 0.14 in (3.5 mm) a month, roughly twice as fast as toenails, which manage about 0.06 in (1.6 mm). Your little fingernail is the slowest of the ten.

Your brain keeps a map of your body. It is wildly out of scale. The hands take up more room on it than your whole trunk and both legs together. The map is drawn by how much control a part needs, not by how big the part is.
more: A surgeon named Wilder Penfield mapped it during operations. His patients were awake. He touched the surface of the brain with a fine wire and asked what they felt, or watched which part of them twitched.

text: Every way you hold anything is one of two grips. A surgeon sorted them out in 1956. In a power grip the fingers wrap round and the palm joins in, the way they do on a hammer. In a precision grip the thing is pinched between thumb and fingertips, the way it is on a pencil.

Your thumb can reach around and touch the tip of every other finger on the same hand. That one trick is the difference between a paddle and a tool-holder: thread a needle, hold a pen, do up a button. It is hard to read a hand as anything but purpose-built.

98.6°F (37°C) is not your temperature. That number came from one German doctor's readings in 1851. Measured today, the average sits closer to 97.9°F (36.6°C), and yours shifts by about a degree over the course of a day all by itself.
tryit: Take your temperature first thing in the morning and again around six in the evening. The evening reading is usually the higher one. Your thermostat runs a schedule, and its lowest point falls in the small hours.

text: Sweat does nothing at all while it is sitting on you. The cooling only happens as it turns into vapor, which is why a muggy day is so much worse than a dry one.
tryit: Wet the back of one hand and leave the other dry, then blow steadily across both. The wet one goes noticeably cold. The water is stealing heat from your skin in order to escape as vapor.
more: You carry somewhere between two and four million sweat glands. Working hard in the heat, a person can pour out a quart or two (1 to 2 liters) an hour. A horse sweats as well. A dog cannot, and has to pant instead.

text: The claim that you lose 40% of your heat through your head is wrong. It traces back to a US Army manual from the 1950s, written after tests where volunteers wore arctic suits with only their heads left bare. Your head is about 7% of your skin, and loses roughly that share.
Shivering is your muscles firing against each other on purpose, making heat instead of movement. Going flat out, it lifts your heat production to around five times its resting level.

The strangest part of a fever is the shivering at the start. The best explanation is that your thermostat has been reset upward, so your ordinary temperature now reads as far too cold. You feel frozen while your body is deliberately running hot.

Every hair on you has a tiny muscle attached that yanks it upright. That is a goosebump. The same muscle fires for cold, for fright and for a piece of music. It doubles as the strut holding a nerve against the cells that grow new hair.
more: Take that muscle away in a mouse and the nerve pulls back and hair growth slows. Leave the mouse in the cold and the nerve fires harder and hair grows faster. The bump you can see is the least of what the muscle is doing.

text: The survivable range for a human core is wider than it looks. Anna Bagenholm was pulled out from under river ice at 56.7°F (13.7°C) with no heartbeat, and lived. Willie Jones survived heatstroke at 115.7°F (46.5°C). Both are records. Both people recovered.

A newborn barely shivers. Instead it carries a special brown fat, stuffed with power plants, across its back and shoulders, and burns it purely to make heat. Most of that fat quietly fades as a child grows.

You have sweat glands all over you, and a thermostat that holds you inside about a degree. That lets a person keep working through the middle of a hot day. Most animals have to find shade. Genesis puts people in a garden to work it and keep it. The cooling kit suits the job.
